entries.paragraph_1: Yet within minutes, the warning evaporated only to be replaced by a cascade of contradictory messages that blamed North Korean planes for an incursion that never happened. South Korean authorities mistook a routine provocation for aÂ complete invasion by North Korea, blaming the wrong country exaggeratedly and entirely. The Russian flyby, the mistaken alerts, and the ensuing confusion reveal deeper rot of a system that conditions populations to fear phantom enemies. Key points: Several Russian military aircraft entered South Korea's air defense identification zone near Ulleung Island prompting a brief emergency alert. South Korean fighter jets scrambled but the aircraft did not violate sovereign airspace. The Interior Ministry issued an evacuation warning that was lifted three minutes later. North Gyeongsang Province mistakenly described the aircraft as suspected North Korean planes using an outdated drill template. South Korea plans to summon a Russian diplomat to lodge a formal protest. The incident follows multiple recent Russian entries into the zone amid heightened Korean Peninsula tensions. AIR RAID evacuation warning turns out to be false alarm When the Interior Ministry's text message hit phones at 7:52 a.m. commanding "EVACUATION, AIR RAID," residents of Ulleung Island had every reason to believe the worst. This is a community still haunted by November 2022 when a North Korean missile screaming toward their island triggered real sirens and civilians scattered with no clue where to seek refuge. But this time the threat was not a missile but a flight of Russian aircraft that never violated South Korean airspace, only its monitoring zone. An air defense identification zone is not sovereign territory but a buffer where a country tracks approaching planes. Russian military aircraft have repeatedly tested this boundary, entering the zone on Nov. 17, Aug. 25 and June 27 of this year alone, according to Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff. Moscow has long rejected the legal basis of South Korea's identification zone and routinely fails to notify Seoul before entering, a practice that turns every approach into a guessing game that ordinary civilians pay for with their peace of mind. The South Korean Air Force scrambled F-15K fighters after detecting the Russian aircraft and conducted tactical maneuvers to prepare for contingencies. A JCS official said the planes flew close to South Korean airspace but moved away toward the East Sea after the military response. The Interior Ministry lifted the alert about three minutes later after the aircraft left the area. Yet those three minutes were enough to expose a deeper dysfunction. The English version of the initial alert read "EVACUATION, AIR RAID," a level far above the precautionary alert the military intended. SBS News reported that the ministry's message erroneously described a flight object presumed to be Russian as having violated airspace, directly contradicting the military's assessment. South Korea blames North Korea for the "invasion" Then came the second and more revealing blunder. At 7:58 a.m., North Gyeongsang Province sent its own cancellation message stating the alert was lifted "because an object presumed to be a North Korean aircraft had left the danger zone." The JoongAng Daily captured the absurdity with its headline questioning whether the aircraft were Russian or North Korean. Provincial officials later admitted they had used an outdated emergency drill template created for a North Korean aircraft scenario. It took approximately 40 minutes before the message was corrected to identify the aircraft as Russian. For the residents of Ulleung Island, who lived through real missile alerts and knew firsthand the terror of not knowing where to run, this bureaucratic theater was worse than incompetence. It was a betrayal of trust. The diplomatic response followed a script as predictable as the provocation itself. South Korea's Defense Ministry announced it would summon a Russian diplomat from the Russian Embassy in Seoul to lodge a formal protest, according to Yonhap News Agency. Yet Russia does not even recognize the legal basis of South Korea's identification zone and has stated clearly that Seoul's claimed control over it lacks foundation in international law. This diplomatic ritual of summoning an ambassador who will reject the protest's premise while the aircraft keep coming has become a meaningless dance. Under standard international practice, military aircraft entering another country's zone submit a flight plan in advance and report their position upon entry. Russia refuses to follow this protocol, and Seoul has no mechanism to compel compliance. The Russian warplanes did not fire a single shot, but they accomplished something far more insidious. They demonstrated that South Korea's defense establishment cannot distinguish a routine incursion from an invasion, cannot issue a clear warning, and cannot even correctly identify which country's aircraft is approaching its shores. When the next emergency comes, and it will, the sirens may sound again, but who will have the confidence to answer them? Sources include: Khaama.com KoreanTimes.co.kr Aljazeera.com

entries.title: North Korea: Nuclear arsenal growth declared irreversible reality in response to US military threats
entries.paragraph_1: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un directed the expansion of the country's nuclear arsenal following an inspection of uranium enrichment facilities, according to state media reports dated November 25, 2026. The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) stated that Kim visited two nuclear materials production factories-one newly inaugurated and the other undergoing expansion-along with a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a research institute. During the tour, Kim declared that the strengthening of North Korea's nuclear capability in both quality and quantity is an "irreversible reality,” citing escalating threats from the United States and South Korea as the primary driver for increased production.
entries.paragraph_2: The decision to expand nuclear capabilities is an executive directive from the Supreme Leader, the highest authority in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Unlike federal legislative processes in the United States, this action does not require approval from a separate branch of government; it is implemented directly through the state's military and industrial apparatus. KCNA's reporting confirms that the directive was issued immediately following the physical inspection of the facilities, signaling a move from strategic planning to active operational expansion. The state's position remains that its nuclear program is a defensive necessity against what it describes as "variable nuclear threats” and U. S. efforts to arm regional allies with nuclear-powered submarines and shared nuclear weapons.

US backs IAEA authority to negotiate South Korean submarine safeguards after China objects
entries.paragraph_1: The United States says the International Atomic Energy Agency, the U.N. nuclear watchdog, has the authority to negotiate safeguards for South Korea’s planned nuclear-powered submarines, a State Department spokesperson told VOA. The statement comes after China objected at an IAEA Board of Governors meeting last week, saying that all of the agency’s member states should agree before such talks proceed. Safeguards are measures the IAEA uses to verify that nuclear material is not diverted for weapons purposes. Nuclear-powered submarines present a particular challenge because their fuel is used for a military activity rather than a peaceful nuclear activity, and the submarines can spend long periods at sea. The United States approved South Korea’s plan to build nuclear-powered submarines in November 2025, but key details, including who will supply the fuel, have not been settled. Under Article 14 of its safeguards agreement with the IAEA, a country without nuclear weapons can reach a separate arrangement with the agency that temporarily suspends normal safeguards on nuclear material used for permitted military purposes, such as powering submarines. At the IAEA board meeting on November 18, China’s ambassador in Vienna, Li Song, said that the way in which the agency monitors nuclear fuel for South Korea’s submarines should be decided by the board and all member states, not only through technical talks between the IAEA and Seoul. He also said U.S.-South Korean cooperation would be the second case, after AUKUS, involving the transfer of nuclear material for non-peaceful purposes. Under AUKUS, a 2021 pact, Britain and the United States are helping Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines. But a State Department spokesperson said in a written response to VOA that the IAEA has established authority to negotiate safeguards implementation, including Article 14 arrangements. U.S. Ambassador Wells Griffith welcomed the technical consultations at the meeting, saying they match the IAEA’s existing authority and South Korea’s Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty obligations. The European Union praised Seoul’s reporting compliance, and the IAEA director general’s report, saying any finalized arrangement would be submitted to the board for appropriate action. An initial IAEA report released November 18 said South Korea plans to manufacture the fuel domestically using imported low-enriched uranium, enriched to 20% or less, without naming a supplier. South Korea and the IAEA held their first technical consultation October 8 and plan to continue talks next year toward an Article 14 arrangement.

entries.title: South Korea's $1 Trillion Export Phenomenon | Armstrong Economics
entries.paragraph_1: South Korea has surpassed $1 trillion in annual exports, becoming only the fourth country in history to reach that milestone, joining the United States, Germany, and China. This is a country that emerged from the Korean War devastated, impoverished, and dependent upon foreign assistance. In the 1960s, Koreans were exporting wigs made from human hair, squid, pig bristles, and whatever else they could sell to earn foreign currency. Today, they are producing the semiconductors powering the global artificial intelligence revolution. This is what happens when a nation develops its productive economy instead of expecting government spending to manufacture prosperity.
entries.paragraph_2: Korean exports have increased more than 36,000-fold since 1948. As recently as 1964, annual exports were only $100 million. They crossed $1 trillion on November 19, 2026, and are projected to reach $1.17 trillion by year-end. The transformation did not happen overnight. South Korea developed steelmaking, shipbuilding, automobiles, electronics, and eventually advanced semiconductors. Its companies invested in manufacturing capabilities that could compete internationally. Samsung, Hyundai, and SK hynix became global industrial powers because they produced goods that consumers and businesses around the world wanted to purchase.

entries.title: US proposes up to 25% ‘excess capacity’ tariff on India, 17% if trade deal is signed | Kashmir Reader
entries.paragraph_1: NEW DELHI: The US on Wednesday proposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in the absence of a trade deal, citing excess industrial capacity, sustained market access barriers and inadequate labour protection that harm American companies. The US Trade Representative (USTR) said the tariffs on India would amount to 17% if it agrees to a trade deal with America. The fresh tariff proposal follows Section 301 investigations launched by the USTR in March targeting 16 economic jurisdictions. The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place. The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15 per cent tariff rates, inclusive of standard import duties. Vietnam would face tariffs of 20 per cent if the trade deal is finalised. “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” said USTR Jamieson Greer. “India generates trade surpluses in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, steel, and ICT goods, revealing dependencies on Indian manufacturing in certain key sectors,” the USTR said in its report on ‘India’s Acts, Policies, and Practices Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors’. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labour or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior US official said. The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and sought written comments from interested persons by January 5. The Office of the USTR has been analysing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favour surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms US industry. The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies imposed by the Trump administration invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labour; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. India and the US are negotiating an interim bilateral trade agreement after the framework they had finalised in February went back to the discussion board with the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs imposed last year. India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. “USTR is applying to India a diagnosis built for a very different economy. India consumes most of what it produces and buys more goods from the world than it sells, so it is not exporting a domestic glut,” said Abhik Sengupta, a Task Force Observer on the Committee on Strategic Trade and Market Access, Helsinki Geoeconomics Society. Sengupta said India’s reliance on Chinese inputs points to gaps in its industrial base, not a surplus. “Penalising India for closing those gaps risks pushing supply chains back toward the very economies Washington is most concerned about,” he said. Trump undeterred by midterms defeat Trump reignited global trade tensions on Wednesday by proposing new tariffs on major trading powers including China, undeterred in his protectionist push by losses by his Republican Party in US midterm elections. His administration proposed levies on 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity. The highest rate of 20% would hit China, which Washington blames for flooding world markets with cheap exports of everything from steel to electric vehicles and solar products. “We know that they don’t like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us,” a senior US official said, adding Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was “really great”. Beijing earlier reiterated its opposition to “trade wars” and dismissed the notion of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation. “The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations. The senior US official said the administration also proposed tariffs on Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway are excluded from new levies. The new duties will take into account any trade deals agreed with the Trump administration and will not stack on top of some previous tariff rounds, suggesting many countries may not see a massive increase in the trading cost with the US. Even so, the prospect of new trade burdens weighed on stock markets on Wednesday as a tech-led rally continued to run out of steam. MSCI’s gauge of stocks around the globe fell 0.5%. “It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING analysts wrote. New duties won’t exceed negotiated limits Trump’s tariffs have contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November’s midterm losses for his Republicans showed 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal them. But Trump has long served notice of a plan to rebuild the duties the US Supreme Court struck down in February. The latest ones come after an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe. The US official also said the new duties would not exceed tariff limits in any trade deals with the Trump administration, including a 20% cap for China during Trump’s second term under a year-old truce with Beijing that is due to expire on January 10. The tariffs would also not apply to about $30 billion worth of Chinese imports that the US is considering for tariff reductions under a bilateral process, the official said. However, they would add to the tariffs on China put in place during Trump’s first term, which amounted to roughly 25%. The proposed duties will further not stack on top of tariffs of 10% or 12.5% that the administration imposed in July on a wider group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labor laws. Specific rates are to be published in a US Federal Register notice on Wednesday. Tariff rates also will be consistent with trade agreements signed by other partners, the official said, including the 15% cap agreed by the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as a 19% cap agreed by Malaysia. The proposed duties will be subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing scheduled before they go into effect. The official said that could push implementation into January. PTI/Reuters

entries.paragraph_1: South Korean Prime Minister Lee Nak-yeon and Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe reached an agreement in a meeting on Oct. 24 that bilateral relations cannot be left in their current strained state. While the two sides did not succeed in bridging their differences over a South Korean Supreme Court ruling ordering compensation for forced labor mobilization during the Japanese occupation of Korea, analysts said they potentially paved the way for restoring senior-level dialogue to reverse the spiral in their relations.
entries.paragraph_2: Lee met with Abe for 21 minutes at the Japanese Prime Minister’s residence in Tokyo’s Chiyoda Ward on the morning of Oct. 24 while visiting Japan to attend its imperial enthronement. The originally scheduled meeting time was around 10 minutes, but the two ended up talking for longer, with Lee delivering a letter to Abe from South Korean President Moon Jae-in. After the meeting, First Vice Foreign Minister Cho Se-young explained, “With regard to South Korea-Japan relations, both prime ministers agreed that the two countries are important neighbors that cannot afford to leave relations in their current difficult state, and they also agreed that non-governmental interchange, including interchange among young people from both countries, is all the more important when the situation is difficult.”

entries.paragraph_2: Lee Sang-ki, THE AsiaN, Korea Chinese Ambassador to South Korea Dai Bing called for stronger bilateral ties during a lecture at Chung-Ang University in Seoul on November 25. Responding to criticism of President Lee Jae-myung as “pro-China,” Dai asked whether maintaining good relations with a large neighboring country could harm South Korea. He urged both sides to remove obstacles to stable cooperation. Addressing concerns that last week’s US-China-Russia summit resembled a new Yalta agreement, Dai rejected the labels “G3” and “Yalta 2.0,” reaffirming China’s commitment to multilateralism. The summit took place in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting. He also supported expanding cultural exchanges while emphasizing respect for China’s sovereignty and fundamental interests.

entries.title: આંતરરાષ્ટ્રીય સરહદ પર યુદ્ધના ભણકારા વચ્ચે સૌથી મોટો અને સનસનાટીભર્યો ધડાકો: રશિયાના વિમાનો દેખાતા સાઉથ કોરિયાએ ફાઈટર જેટ્સ ઉડાવ્યા: ટાપુ ખાલી કરવાનું એલર્ટ આપી માત્ર ૩ મિનિટમાં પાછું ખેંચતા ભારે હાહાકાર
entries.paragraph_1: નવી દિલ્હી : આંતરરાષ્ટ્રીય સ્તરે તણાવભરી પરિસ્થિતિ વચ્ચે સાઉથ કોરિયા માં એક એવી સનસનાટીભરી ઘટના બની છે , જેણે ક્ષણભરમાં યુદ્ધ જેવો માહોલ સર્જી દીધો હતો . રશિયાના વિમાનો દેખાતા સાઉથ કોરિયાએ તાત્કાલિક પોતાના ફાઈટર જેટ્સ આકાશમાં ઉડાવ્યા હતા અને સાવચેતીના ભાગરૂપે ટાપુ ખાલી કરવાનું એલર્ટ જારી કર્યું હતું , પરંતુ માત્ર ૩ મિનિટ બાદ આ એલર્ટ પાછું ખેંચી લેવામાં આવતા ભારે હડકંપ અને ચકચાર મચી ગઈ છે . એર ડિફેન્સ આઇડેન્ટિફિકેશન ઝોન એ કોઈપણ દેશ દ્વારા પોતાની હવાઈ સીમાની સુરક્ષા માટે નક્કી કરવામાં આવેલો એક ખાસ વિસ્તાર છે . આ ઝોનની મદદથી દેશની હવાઈ સીમા તરફ આવી રહેલા કોઈપણ અજાણ્યા કે વિદેશી વિમાનની સમયસર ઓળખ કરી શકાય છે અને જરૂર પડ્યે તાત્કાલિક જવાબી કાર્યવાહી કરી શકાય છે . આ ઘટના પહેલા સાઉથ કોરિયાના સુરક્ષા મંત્રાલયે પૂર્વ કિનારે આવેલા ઉલેઉંગ ટાપુ (Ulleung island) માટે ખાલી કરવાની ચેતવણી ( ઇવેક્યુએશન વોર્નિંગ ) જાહેર કરી હતી . મંત્રાલયે તે સમયે કહ્યું હતું કે એક રશિયન વિમાન દેશની હવાઈ સીમામાં પ્રવેશ્યું છે . જોકે , માત્ર ત્રણ મિનિટ બાદ આ ચેતવણી પાછી ખેંચી લેવામાં આવી હતી . સ્થાનિક ન્યૂઝ એજન્સી ' યોનહાપ ' ના અહેવાલ મુજબ , સ્થાનિક પ્રશાસન દ્વારા ભૂલથી ઉલેઉંગ વિસ્તાર નજીક ઉત્તર કોરિયાનું વિમાન હોવાની ચેતવણી પણ થોડીવાર માટે જાહેર થઈ ગઈ હતી , જેને બાદમાં રદ કરવામાં આવી હતી .
entries.paragraph_2: નવી દિલ્હી : આંતરરાષ્ટ્રીય સ્તરે તણાવભરી પરિસ્થિતિ વચ્ચે સાઉથ કોરિયા માં એક એવી સનસનાટીભરી ઘટના બની છે , જેણે ક્ષણભરમાં યુદ્ધ જેવો માહોલ સર્જી દીધો હતો . રશિયાના વિમાનો દેખાતા સાઉથ કોરિયાએ તાત્કાલિક પોતાના ફાઈટર જેટ્સ આકાશમાં ઉડાવ્યા હતા અને સાવચેતીના ભાગરૂપે ટાપુ ખાલી કરવાનું એલર્ટ જારી કર્યું હતું , પરંતુ માત્ર ૩ મિનિટ બાદ આ એલર્ટ પાછું ખેંચી લેવામાં આવતા ભારે હડકંપ અને ચકચાર મચી ગઈ છે .

entries.title: Russia sends 3 messages at once with strategic bomber flight near South Korea
entries.paragraph_1: Russian supersonic strategic bombers came within seconds of entering South Korean airspace near Ulleung Island on Tuesday in an unprecedented move that is raising questions about Moscow’s intentions. Russian military aircraft enter Korea’s air defense identification zone (KADIZ) several dozen times a year, but never before has a nuclear-capable strategic bomber come so close to Korean airspace. Some analysts believe Russia was seeking to demonstrate its commitment to its alliance with North Korea. According to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, a Russian strategic bomber formation entered the KADIZ around 7:40 am on Tuesday and flew south toward Ulleung Island. By 7:52 am, the aircraft had approached within 13 nautical miles of the island and just 1 nautical mile from the boundary of Korean airspace. Another two or three seconds of flight would have taken them into Korean airspace. The South Korean military responded by scrambling several F-15K fighter jets. Russia’s Defense Ministry identified the aircraft flying over the East Sea that day as Tu-160 strategic bombers conducting a scheduled flight over international waters, according to Russia’s TASS news agency. The flight lasted approximately 10 hours, with the bombers escorted by Su-35S and Su-30SM fighter jets from the Russian Aerospace Forces. The Russian Defense Ministry said its aircraft strictly comply with international rules on the use of airspace in all flights. The Tu-160 is a supersonic long-range strategic bomber capable of carrying nuclear missiles, with a maximum range of over 12,000 kilometers. Its all-white paint scheme has earned it the moniker “White Swan.” The formation that entered KADIZ consisted of four aircraft: two Tu-160 bombers with an escort of one Su-35S and one Su-30SM fighter. Korea’s Defense Ministry summoned the Russian defense attaché, a colonel in the air force, to lodge a protest. The Foreign Ministry did not summon the Russian ambassador but expressed regret through diplomatic channels and urged Moscow to ensure that such an incident is not repeated. Russia’s Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, announced that Korean Ambassador to Russia Lee Sok-bae had met with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko to discuss pressing issues.
entries.paragraph_2: The incident was unusual in several respects. For one thing, the nuclear-capable Tu-160 strategic bomber has never before made an appearance over the East Sea (also called the Sea of Japan). Known as the world’s largest supersonic strategic bomber, the Tu-160 can carry air-launched cruise missiles fitted with nuclear warheads and reach speeds of around Mach 2. Russia gave North Korean leader Kim Jong-un a tour of its strategic bombers, including the Tu-160, during his visit to Vladivostok in September 2023. Russia has sent Tu-95MS bombers into the KADIZ on multiple previous occasions. But on this occasion, it sent the supersonic Tu-160 to the very edge of South Korean airspace, cranking up the pressure on Seoul. Russian military aircraft have recently passed through the KADIZ on their way to Japan’s air defense identification zone. This time, however, the Russian aircraft did not continue toward Japan after narrowly skirting South Korean airspace over Ulleung Island, suggesting that the operation was aimed specifically at South Korea. Experts believe Russia’s primary objective was to demonstrate to North Korea that it is fulfilling its obligations under their Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, while also using the show of force to put pressure on the South Korean government. Russia and North Korea’s treaty, signed in June 2024, pledges mutual military assistance. Russian President Vladimir Putin emphasized the two countries’ brotherhood in arms and their commitment to the treaty in a meeting with Jo Yong-won, a senior official in North Korea’s ruling party, on Nov. 16. “The fact that Russia’s strategic bombers only brushed by South Korea this time without continuing on to Japan suggests that the operation was intended to send a message to both South and North Korea,” said Doo Jin-ho, a visiting research fellow at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies. “North Korea has sent combat troops to Russia, but Russia hadn’t previously rotated strategic assets into the region. It apparently wanted to show the North that it’s honoring its defense commitments,” Doo said. Lee Byong-chul, a professor at the same institute, said that Russia was “visibly demonstrating its commitment to defending North Korea under their bilateral treaty while also providing deterrence against the South Korea-US alliance and signaling that it could intervene in a contingency on the Korean Peninsula.” “Just as the US deploys strategic weapons to the Korean Peninsula under its mutual defense treaty with South Korea, Russia may continue deploying strategic weapons in the future as North Korea’s military backer,” Lee said.
